articles.title: GRSE Signs Contract With ONGC to Build Four Vessels
articles.text:
Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Ltd. (GRSE), a Navratna Defence Public Sector Undertaking under the Ministry of Defence, Government of India, has signed a contract with Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC) for the construction of four Hybrid Platform Supply Vessels (PSVs), marking a significant step forward in the shipyard’s foray into specialised offshore support vessels. The contract follows the Notification of Award received by GRSE on 30 July 2026.
The contract was signed by Cdr Shantanu Bose, IN(Retd), Director (Shipbuilding), GRSE, and Shri Ratnesh Kumar, Executive Director (Strategy), ONGC, in the presence of Shri Satyen Kumar, Director (Technical), ONGC, Shri Bhaskar Chowdary Nettem, Director (Production), ONGC, and senior officials from GRSE & ONGC.
The project marks an important addition to GRSE’s commercial shipbuilding portfolio, extending its capabilities in the specialised offshore support vessel segment. The vessels will support ONGC’s offshore exploration and production operations, contributing to the maritime infrastructure required by India’s energy sector.
With an overall length of approximately 80 metres, a beam of 20 metres and a deadweight capacity of 3,000 tonnes, each vessel will feature a clear deck area of around 650 square metres and an endurance of 45+3 days. Designed and built in accordance with the Rules of the Indian Register of Shipping (IRS), the vessels will be equipped to undertake a range of offshore logistics and support functions.
A defining feature of the project is the incorporation of an advanced hybrid propulsion architecture, comprising electrically driven azimuth thrusters and a Lithium-Ion Battery Energy Storage System. The battery system will support peak load management, spinning reserve, dynamic positioning operations and emergency response functions. This configuration is intended to enhance operational efficiency and reduce the environmental impact of vessel operations.
The ONGC contract represents a further step in diversifying GRSE’s order portfolio and applying its shipbuilding expertise to the requirements of the commercial maritime and offshore energy sectors.

articles.title: Fatah-2 ER: How Pakistan Is Seeking to Overcome India’s Air Defences
articles.text:
On 13 October 2026, the Fatah-2 missile was tested with an extended range by Pakistan’s Army Rocket Force Command as part of its efforts to launch its first hypersonic ballistic missile that can penetrate enemy missile defence systems with its “unique trajectory” and manoeuvrability, ISPR said. The test follows a long-range Fatah-IV cruise missile test a week ago, indicating Islamabad is steadily expanding its conventional strike arsenal. But how much of this is true and how is India getting ready?
For some perspective, head back to May 2025. Pakistan allegedly fired a Fatah-II towards the Delhi region that was intercepted over Sirsa (Haryana) on 10 May during the four-day conflict, as part of Operation Sindoor. The Indian system which made the kill is not yet officially confirmed — reports variously say it was either Barak-8 or MR-SAM, or S-400 or even Akash-NG. Even the targeting is an assessment, not a certainty — the missile “may have had Delhi as its target”, officials said, and debris came down around Sirsa and Jalandhar. That much is certain – the base Fatah-II, despite the excitement was downed.
The Fatah-II is no blueprint. It is a quasi-ballistic surface-to-surface missile with domestic range of approximately 400 km, 365 kg warhead, 600 mm diameter and INS-plus-GNSS guidance system with all course manoeuvrability. It is designed and built at home by NESCOM and GIDS, and equipped with Chinese Taian eight-wheel chassis. It is often elaborated into a neat story that Pakistan went to Beijing and brought back an ER missile. That’s not proven. The ER version is apparently the same 600 mm diameter, but just longer, as indicated by the footages released so far. The connection with the Chinese in the Fatah family is genuine, but a Chinese hand in this particular variant is speculation.
So how Pakistan is trying to beat Indian’s air defence? Not one wonder weapon but three things at once. One, trajectory shaping — a flat, depressed, quasi-ballistic trajectory, with manoeuvring, was intended to try to avoid the defender having a predictable intercept solution, and to reduce reaction time. Three, mass — the Pakistani commentary, which likens Iran’s barrage on Israel, is saturated with volume. To this must be added the Army Rocket Force Command established after Sindoor to safeguard Indian air bases, logistics centres and long-range air-defence systems.
India’s response is multi-layered and growingly homegrown. The current shield covers the Russian S-400 at 400 km; the Barak-8 or MR-SAM in the 70-150 km range; and the Akash-NG, Spyder, QRSAM and VSHORADS, which cover the very long-range portion. Project Kusha is supposed to fill the gap between the MR-SAM and the S-400, which is effectively three interceptors – M1 at 150 km, M2 at 250 km, M3 at 350 to 400 km. The first test is expected to be undertaken on 23 July 2026 and induction is planned for 2028-30. Interestingly, Kusha is designed to be capable of dealing with manoeuvring and hypersonic threats, including dual RF/IR technology to penetrate countermeasures. Below is the indigenous two-tier ballistic missile defence system, Phase-I has been validated and Phase-II is in development. Nestled amidst all this is Mission Sudarshan Chakra, which Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced in August 2025 to create an integrated, multi-layered shield by 2035.
Most importantly, India is not counting on interceptors completely. They focus on integration and redundancy—networked sensors, AI-based data fusion and the IAF’s Integrated Air Command and Control System—as if-good-interceptors fail under saturation, there’s no need for seamless cueing. There is a sword to match – the Army chief has been pushing for a dedicated rocket and missile force based on the Pralay, BrahMos, ITCM of 1,000 km and the long-range Pinaka.
This is a solved problem, no, it’s a spiral. There is no published flight data available for Pakistan’s “defeat any missile defence” line, as one Fatah-II missile was already intercepted in 2025. However, India’s shield that has performed well in a short conflict will require much more number of launchers and interceptor stockpiles in a longer conflict and integration, not any single missile, is the true test.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: ISRO Develops LOX-Methane Engine Technology for Future Rockets
articles.text:
Liquid propulsion activities in ISRO had a humble beginning with development and delivery of small thrusters for SLV-3 and Secondary Injection Thrust Vector Control (SITVC) systems and later delivery of similar control system for ASLV. A quantum jump in liquid propulsion came through the collaborative development of the 800kN Vikas engine for PSLV, which is today the workhorse liquid engine of ISRO used in PSLV, GSLV & LVM3. Subsequently, India mastered the much-coveted Cryogenic propulsion by developing indigenous cryogenic engines & stages for the GSLV and LVM3 launch vehicles, thereby making the nation self-reliant in launching communication satellites. Similarly, on the satellite front, ISRO started with the development & delivery of monopropellant thrusters, moved on to bi-propellant Liquid Apogee Motors (LAM) needed for the INSAT communication satellites. ISRO has also developed throttle-able propulsion systems for Chandrayaan-3 lander mission that enabled the nation to be the first to land a spacecraft near the south pole of the Moon.
Globally, liquid propulsion systems have witnessed a shift towards LOX-Methane engines, considering the clean combustion, low maintenance (useful for reusability) and the ability to be synthesized on Mars from CO2 and water ice (useful for future Mars missions and human colonization). In this context, ISRO has also identified LOX-Methane engines as the primary propulsion systems for its Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV) and also the future heavy lift launch vehicle required for the Indian crewed lunar landing mission targeted for 2040.
Considering the potential of LOX-Methane propulsion systems in future launch vehicles, ISRO initiated development activities in this area in 2019, to understand critical aspects of liquid oxygen–liquid methane (LOX-methane) propellants combination on engine operation. A a 20-ton thrust technology demonstrator engine (designated as LM20-TD engine) was developed & tested using the existing CE-20 LOX/LH2 cryogenic engine subsystems during the 2019-2020 timeframe. Suitable modifications were carried out in the propellant flow control system and the engine start-up system of CE20 engine to convert the engine to the demonstrator engine. The demonstrator engine operated on the gas generator cycle with major subsystems including Thrust Chamber, fuel rich gas generator, Fuel Turbopump, LOX Turbopump, Igniter, Start-up system, Control components, Flow control elements, mixture ratio control valve with electric drive. The design adequacy of all subsystems was assessed through theoretical analysis prior to the development tests. Test sequence was derived using an in-house developed mathematical model.
The existing cryogenic engine test facility at IPRC was augmented for the purpose of testing the LM20 demonstrator engine and one cold flow test and five hot tests were carried out successfully. With the data obtained from these tests, vital inputs were derived on chill down characteristics, thrust chamber and gas generator ignition, engine starting, combustion and rotor-dynamic systems performance for a LOX- Methane engine.
The inputs derived from the Technology Demonstrator engine have been gainfully utilized in the design of LOX-Methane engine that is under development in ISRO.
Hot test of Technology Demonstrator Engine (LM20-TD) at IPRC
In 2023, ISRO formally initiated the development of key technologies for a 1100kN LOX-Methane engine (LME1100), that focused on the development & validation of key technologies leading to the different subsystems of the engine viz. turbopumps, igniter, gas generator and thrust chamber.
LME1100 engine is designed as a Gas Generator Cycle (GGC) based engine where the design is optimized for industry friendliness and cost effectiveness. With the active involvement of industrial partners across the nation, more than 70% of the LME1100 engine components have been realized through Additive Manufacturing.
The Gas Generator (GG) is realized through additive manufacturing and is under qualification tests at IPRC. The sub-scale version was subjected to extensive testing at lab level to derive the ignition sequence using the spark torch igniter and to characterize the additively manufactured injector elements during ignition. The first ignition test of the full-scale Gas Generator was successfully carried out on October 9, 2026 and a series of similar tests are planned to evaluate the performance under different conditions.
Sub-scale thrust chamber hot test campaign was also carried out. The test series was used to demonstrate the novel realization techniques planned to be eventually adopted in the full scale thrust chamber. The hot test campaign was also used to characterize the injector elements designed for LME1100 thrust chamber in actual operating conditions for varying design and operating parameters. The hot test campaign carried out at IPRC not only helped in finalizing the optimal injector configuration, but also helped in demonstrating the working of oxidizer rich and fuel rich spark torch igniters.
The LOX and Methane turbo-pump systems are also realized through various industries across the nation and the hardware are under different levels of sub-system testing at LPSC and IPRC. The 3D printed LOX pump impeller was subjected to spin test up to the rated operating speed at LPSC. Dynamic sealing systems and turbo-pump bearings have also been realized through Indian industries and are under qualification testing at LPSC and IPRC. Cold flow characterization of the integrated turbo-pump systems are under progress at IPRC.
The sub-system testing activities were initiated with the ignition trials and extensive testing of the GOX-GCH4 based spark torch igniter. Both oxidizer rich and fuel rich versions of spark torch igniters were developed and tested successfully. Alternatively, an igniter using a semiconductor-based spark plug was also developed by LPSC along with VSSC and the Indian Institute of Space Science & Technology (IIST). Laser based ignition system has also been developed at LPSC and has been successfully demonstrated in igniting GOX-GH2 and GOX-GCH4 propellant combinations.
The integrated LME1100 engine is targeted to be ready by the middle of next year and will be subjected to a series of hot tests to qualify the same for the prescribed operating conditions including different thrust throttling profiles. Concurrently, the design activities towards the development of a 2400kN LOX-Methane engine are also completed, which is based on the Full Flow Staged Combustion Cycle (FFSCC). The 2400kN engine will enable the development of a future heavy lift human rated launch vehicle for crewed lunar landing missions.

articles.title: Su-57 for India? Why Russia Is Watching China’s J-35 Moves
articles.text:
The debate rages on in Delhi, but the real battle may be in Beijing. That is the curious context in which India’s fifth-generation fighter jet dilemma must be understood. The outcome of the competition between the indigenous AMCA and the Russian Su-57 may depend less on the relative merits of the two aircraft and more on whether China decides to sell Pakistan its J-35 stealth fighter or honour the 16 J-10CE fighters Islamabad has purchased but not paid for.
The IAF is far from being unanimous on the issue. While the outgoing chief, Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh, has warned that if the AMCA goes awry, the IAF “may have to look at other options” (Russia’s Su-57 among them), his successor, Air Chief Marshal Harpal Singh, has not been so vocal. During his press briefing last week, the incoming chief confirmed that the AMCA project is “on track”, but said nothing of other possibilities. Air Chief Marshal Singh’s comments come in response to Pakistani media reports that Pakistan is buying Chinese stealth fighters and has begun training its pilots in their use. They also follow statements by Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh that India has “not opted for any foreign fifth-generation fighter aircraft” – “our programme is AMCA” – and that New Delhi has “placed all its eggs in this basket”. Singh has also consistently supported the 114-Rafale MRFA deal, and has previously said that new Sukhois are not an option, while the Super Sukhoi upgrade is.
The reason why the debate about the Su-57 has even cropped up in the first place is China. It was revealed last month that Beijing has halted deliveries of the 16 J-10CE fighters Pakistan has ordered – due to Islamabad’s inability to pay installments on the deal. With an initial order of 36 planes plus 250 PL-15 missiles, with the proceeds from the first 20 planes (mostly paid for by loans from China), the Pakistani government finds itself in the position of wanting more J-10CEs, but being unable to pay for them.
Much more interesting, however, is the situation surrounding the J-35. Pakistan has reportedly signed an “initial collaborative agreement” for the stealth fighter, with a total of 40 J-35A aircraft potentially on order, with the PAF sending pilots to China for training in the meantime – despite no actual sale having been concluded. The most plausible reason why the deal has not been finalised is because the J-35 is the only fifth-generation fighter China is capable of operating from its carriers, and Beijing will likely want to keep some aircraft for itself. With three carriers already under construction, and plans for building more, it is unlikely that China will be able to divert any of the J-35s it is building for Pakistan before 2027 at the earliest. Meanwhile, Pakistan’s financial situation means that it will be hard-pressed to make any further payments towards the J-10CE order, let alone fund a new order for stealth fighters.
This is the context in which Su-57 must be viewed. With India waiting for the AMCA to come online, and Pakistan waiting for China to deliver on its J-35 promise, the IAF is likely to find itself with a “fifth-generation gap” in the years between 2027 and 2030. AMCA is unlikely to see combat before the mid-2030s at the earliest – its first prototype is not due to fly before 2029, and the project has a long way to go before private companies can be invited to participate. If the PAF receives the J-35 in 2030, the IAF will only have five years between losing its fifth-gen aircraft to the PAF and potentially receiving the AMCA, if it comes online on schedule. If China decides to accelerate the delivery of the J-35 and deliver it to Pakistan by 2027, the “gap” will stretch to eight years. Meanwhile, if the timeline for the AMCA slips – and there is every reason to believe it might – the situation will be even worse. With the IAF currently having only 29 squadrons compared to the sanctioned 42.5, and its chief complaining that the service only has enough aircraft to fund 36-40 new jet fighters per year, India cannot afford to wait much longer.
For Russia, however, the Su-57 deal is a no-brainer. Moscow wants the deal to go through, both because the money would be most welcome in the Russian defense industry – the Russian defense budget has been severely constrained by the war in Ukraine – and because the technology transfer deal it has proposed to India would solve a long-standing problem for the Russian defense industry. Russia has offered India license production of the Su-57 in India, wide technology transfers to local firms, access to source code, and the integration of Indian weapons into the Russian fifth-gen fighter. Meanwhile, a Russian delegation has already visited Nashik to size up the facilities for the Su-57 project.
India’s options in fifth-gen fighters are limited, but the Su-57 deal is a crucial choice that reflects both the urgency and the strategic importance of the issue. If China does not deliver on the J-35 and Pakistan’s payments for the J-10CEs dry up, Delhi will have no problem waiting for the AMCA to come online. However, if the PAF manages to acquire a stealth aircraft from China, the divided Indian defense establishment may have to decide quickly what to do next – to the relief of Russia, which has invested much in promoting the Su-57 deal.

articles.title: Cybercrims go beyond stealing data to attack physical building systems
articles.text: Late Sunday night, a still-unknown cybercriminal or group hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of French grocery stores, spiking temperatures, spoiling food, and sparking fires. This is part of an ongoing trend of attacking physical systems that can do damage in the real world. In August, a ransomware attack disrupted building-management systems at a Canadian hospital, affecting door access controls, central HVAC monitoring, and the issuing of staff access cards. And three years ago, cyberattacks hit Las Vegas casinos, causing slot machines to go dark, preventing payment kiosks and ATMs from spitting out cash, and locking guests out of their rooms when the electronic keys stopped working. Not all digital intrusions remain in cyberspace, and attackers don’t need to encrypt files and steal data to cause chaos. Hitting physical systems often produces more severe consequences - and turns up the heat on executives to pay an extortion demand. “There was one gig where the customer was refusing to pay, and so the threat actor was like, ‘Hold my beer, have fun getting into your offices,’ and locked everybody out,” Tim Beasley, a senior incident response consultant at Semperis, told The Register. Beasley won’t name the customer, or provide any incriminating information, but said the incident response involved police smashing glass in addition to his team recovering compromised data. “The cops had to break in, and literally get into the building, breaking some windows, so the customer was able to finally get back in,” he said. We asked if the customer paid the ransom demand, and Beasley yelled: “Oh, hell, no!” A report published earlier this month by ServiceNow’s Armis Labs found increasing evidence of ransomware attackers using physical consequences as leverage in their intrusions. “Today’s BAS operate at the intersection of IT and OT worlds, creating unprecedented exposure,” the report said. Ransomware with physical consequences Building automation systems - BAS - are the critical systems that control and monitor facilities’ HVAC, lighting, energy usage, and water consumption. They also oversee badge readers, door locks, surveillance cameras, fire alarm control panels, and other physical safety equipment. As such, BAS make very attractive targets for ransomware operators looking for high-pressure ways to extort organizations into paying multi-million ransom demands. These systems also appeal to government-backed goons and hacktivists looking to ensure maximum psychological and physical impact during destructive cyberattacks. Armis Labs found 73 percent of organizations own BAS that have been used in ransomware attacks, and this same percentage have known exploited vulnerabilities in at least one of their building automation systems. Additionally, 91 percent of BAS communicate over insecure protocols - opening up an even bigger attack surface for cyber-miscreants wanting to cause physical harm. “The primary thing that we see with any attack on building management systems or physical systems: It’s a great place for the threat actor to hide,” Michael Freeman, ServiceNow’s senior director of threat research, told The Register. “It's easier for them to compromise, and it's easier for them to hide in.” BAS and operational technology (OT) in general have fewer security controls than IT systems. Most require continual uptime, which makes them harder to patch or even scan for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations as this may lead to outages. “One case in particular, against a very large financial institution, the threat actors were staying low and quiet by attacking their BMS systems, and then pivoting into the IT environment,” Freeman said. The intruders were routinely caught - and booted from - the financial institution’s IT systems, so they built backdoors into the BMS to ensure persistent access to both OT and IT networks. “We're also seeing threat actors using AI to understand more building automation systems, especially ones that are using obscure OSs like VxWorks, older Unix-type systems,” Freeman said. AI has entered the chat As multiple security experts have told us in previous interviews, security through obscurity is dead. Not only does AI make it easier for attackers to find bugs – some very obscure and decades old - but it also means criminals no longer need to be OT experts to carry out destructive cyberattacks on critical networks and facilities. Instead, they can use AI to learn all about the obscure protocols and proprietary hardware and software that historically made industrial control systems black boxes. “It’s easier to understand what the controls are,” Freeman said, using the example of an attacker trying to take down a plane, or some similar catastrophic cyberattack. Historically, even advanced, government-backed hacking squads would “be quiet, because you don't know what changing certain settings is going to do,” Freeman explained. “Now you can use AI to say, ‘If I compromise a weight and balance system for airlines, all I need to do now is move this number here to this number, and I just told the system to load heavy stuff on the right side of the plane instead of equal distribution.'” Freeman told us he has seen attackers break into airlines’ OT gear in the past. “But they didn’t know what they were getting into, and so they left them alone,” he said. “Those do cause me concern because in the past I've helped to kick people out of those types of systems.” Industrial orgs increasingly under attack OT security provider Dragos tracks ransomware groups’ claims against industrial organizations on the criminals’ leak sites, along with publicly disclosed intrusions affecting manufacturing and other critical sectors. To be clear: claims on leak sites aren’t always accurate or even true, and the claim itself doesn’t mean operations or control systems were hit. Since 2022, however, “the numbers have been consistently increasing,” Lexie Mooney, senior threat analyst at Dragos, told The Register. The cybersecurity firm tracked 995 ransomware attacks against industrial orgs in 2023, a 49.5 percent increase from 2022. That number jumped more than 87 percent in 2024. Active ransomware groups targeting industrial orgs also grew in 2024 to 80 groups, up from 50 the year before. Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups impacting more than 3,300 industrial organizations in 2025, and the incidents have steadily increased every quarter this year: 1,020 incidents in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,140 incidents in Q2. “The vast majority of cases are opportunistic,” Abdul Alamri, a senior threat analyst at Dragos, told us. “In some of the cases that we have seen an operational impact, either physical systems or an OT operation, it’s just the nature of the opportunism on the part of those ransomware groups.” This is partially due to the complexity of OT systems, he added. “Ransomware groups want to disrupt operations, and put pressure on the victims to pay the ransom,” Alamri said. “They don’t want to invest that time and effort to target complex systems." It’s usually quicker and easier for financially motivated crims to affect operations via IT systems - as the extortionists did in the August 2025 Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) breach, which halted manufacturing and crippled business operations for months. Internet-connected OT: the next 'low-hanging fruit' The other side of this complexity, however, is that many organizations themselves still lack visibility into their OT environments. Dragos estimates that fewer than 10 percent of OT networks worldwide currently have sufficient network monitoring in place. Plus, in 30 percent of incidents the security firm responded to in 2025, the investigations did not begin with a detection alert, but with someone noticing that “something seemed wrong” in operations. This lack of visibility, combined with threats from AI, worries Alamri. “If you compare the risk that we have seen from humans, to what we are about to face in the near future with AI agents who might continuously try to break into those systems - it’s a pretty dark future if we don't take the right measures to protect ourselves against it.” As organizations get better at patching and securing IT systems, attackers will likely look to internet-connected OT systems where digital compromises have real-world consequences, according to Matt Hayden, VP of cyber and emerging threats at General Dynamics Information Technology. “We all anticipate that as we get better at reducing the IT low-hanging fruit, OT will become a vector of much more scrutiny and much more attention,” Hayden told The Register. Before joining GDIT, Hayden served as the assistant secretary for cyber, infrastructure, risk and resilience policy at the US Department of Homeland Security. Compliance vs. security “There is a big focus on the hardware being connected for the purpose of compliance - and to make sure that, in the name of compliance, we aren't opening back doors, to devices that traditionally wouldn't have to be connected to facilitate their service,” he said, using refrigeration units as an example of one such system that is now internet-connected for compliance purposes. This was prior to the French supermarket hacks. Refrigeration units’ monitoring systems connect to the internet so their owners and operators can prove to regulators that the units maintain their uptime and temperature in accordance with regulations. “So if the health department comes by, they say, ‘Look, my refrigerator was at 27 degrees for the last 72 days,' and they have a check mark, and they get their A plus. But that simple connectivity is also a vector in which that particular refrigerant unit could be targeted for disruption,” Hayden said. About a week after our interview, criminals did exactly that. “The recently reported exploitations of commercial refrigeration units represent a significant example of devices without digital value, no sensitive data or extended enterprise access, being exploited by being connected to the internet with unpatched firmware,” Hayden told us in a subsequent email. He said he expects the attribution to be “less nation-state, and more likely those looking for targets of opportunity to identify what could be done with the unpatched systems.” “The consequences are food supply degradation at a small scale, but it is an important example of what could happen at scale very quickly with more consequential operating equipment,” Hayden said.®

articles.title: DRDO Seeks Digital Twin for Aero Engine Health Monitoring
articles.text:
The DRDO has invited Indian companies, startups and MSMEs to develop a digital twin framework for an aero engine Health and Usage Monitoring System (HUMS), a project set to combine physics-based modelling, AI and engine test data to monitor gas turbine performance and detect abnormalities. The initiative is being pursued under the DRDO’s Technology Development Fund (TDF) scheme through grant-in-aid support.
The request for a proposal, issued by the Directorate of Technology Development Fund at DRDO Bhawan in New Delhi, calls for a digital twin for an aero gas turbine engine designated by the Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE), a DRDO laboratory. The framework is expected to replicate the engine’s physical behaviour in a virtual space, enabling engineers to study the engine’s subsystems, monitor operating parameters and evaluate performance under different conditions.
The project calls for a hybrid modelling approach. Physics-based thermodynamic models will be combined with data-driven models developed using engine test results to improve the accuracy of the virtual representation. The framework is also expected to operate in real time on a suitable computing platform, integrating engine models, simulation outputs and sensor information.
Artificial intelligence-augmented thermodynamic modelling and virtual sensors have been identified as key technologies. The virtual sensors are set to derive or estimate parameters that cannot be measured directly, while sensor validation and recovery functions will help identify unreliable readings and support monitoring. The system is expected to identify suitable sensor types, quantities and locations for monitoring the engine through its service life.
The tender calls for a comprehensive package rather than a standalone software model. Deliverables include the hybrid digital twin, computing hardware, real-time operating capabilities, sensor validation and recovery systems, virtual sensor algorithms, a fault and alarm framework, and a graphical user interface. The interface is set to display warnings and alarms, present engine components visually and support data storage and retrieval.
The development schedule extends across 30 months, with four principal milestones. The first six months are set to be devoted to requirements definition, architecture selection and preliminary design review. By the 12-month mark, the development agency is expected to complete detailed design work, collect and preprocess data from 50 to 60 engine tests and demonstrate an integrated engineering prototype incorporating 17 digital-twin blocks.
The 18-month milestone covers prototype development, initial source code, testing and validation reports, and verification against experimental or synthesised engine data. By 30 months, the project is set to deliver the integrated hardware and software platform, validated source code, acceptance-test documentation and user manuals. The schedule is also set to include training models using ground tests, simulated-altitude tests and flight-test data.
The DRDO has specified safeguards for sensitive engine information. Experimental data will be shared with the selected development agency for evaluation at DRDO-defined premises, but engine-run data will not be shared with the industrial partner outside those premises. Changes to the framework involving this data will also be undertaken at DRDO facilities in consultation with its team.

articles.title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
articles.text:
Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives.

Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.

Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect, communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.

articles.title: Rising borrowing costs signal funding risks for global AI expansion: Jefferies report
articles.text: Financial markets are showing signs of increasing stress in funding the global artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom, with borrowing risks rising for companies involved in building AI infrastructure, according to a Jefferies research report.The report highlighted a sharp increase in credit risk indicators for companies such as Oracle and CoreWeave, raising concerns over whether financial markets will continue to support the massive investments required for AI expansion.In its GREED & fear research report titled "K-shaped stresses, AI tremors and the Houthis," Jefferies' Christopher Wood said investors should closely monitor borrowing conditions as companies continue to spend heavily on AI infrastructure.The report said investors need to remain "laser focused on credit spreads for any evidence that the market is no longer willing to fund the ongoing AI capex boom".Credit spreads are indicators of the risk associated with lending to companies. A rise in these spreads generally signals that investors are demanding greater compensation for taking on credit risk.According to the report, Oracle's five-year credit default swap (CDS) spread increased from 186 basis points on September 11 to 288 basis points, while CoreWeave's spread surged from 749 basis points to 1,118 basis points during the same period."These are the highest levels seen so far since the AI capex cycle got underway in early 2023," the report noted.It also highlighted that the yield on CoreWeave's bond maturing in 2032 had reached 14.8 per cent, indicating elevated financing costs for the company.The development is significant as expanding AI infrastructure requires substantial investments in data centres, computing capacity and related technology. Higher borrowing costs could make financing such projects more challenging, particularly for companies dependent on external funding.However, the report does not suggest that funding for AI projects has stopped. Instead, it identifies rising credit risk as an early warning sign that investors should monitor.Jefferies also highlighted the possibility of slowing earnings growth among AI-related companies. Citing a separate research report titled "Diversifying Beyond AI," published on October 13, it said consensus earnings growth for global AI stocks is expected to moderate from around 100 per cent in 2026 to 30 per cent in 2027 and 22 per cent in 2028.The report noted that global AI stocks trade at 23 times forward earnings, compared with 13 times for non-AI stocks, reflecting a considerable valuation gap.The findings suggest that although investment in AI remains substantial, rising financing risks and expectations of slower earnings growth could increase pressure on companies to justify their spending.

articles.title: AI race may depend more on access to power, infrastructure than chip supply: Morgan Stanley
articles.text: The global race to expand artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities could increasingly be determined by which companies can secure enough electricity, financing and data-centre infrastructure to operate advanced chips, rather than simply by their ability to acquire the latest technology, according to a Morgan Stanley research report.The assessment comes as rapid investment in AI infrastructure threatens to outpace the availability of electricity, raising concerns that smaller companies could struggle to compete with financially stronger technology giants.In its equity research report titled "What Does the Power Shortfall Mean for Semis?", Morgan Stanley estimated that US data-centre developers could face a 32-gigawatt (GW) power shortfall through 2028, even after accounting for additional power-generation solutions. This represents around 34 per cent of projected power requirements.The report said, "Nvidia confirmed our thesis that there is not enough power to meet demand, and there are more semiconductors being built than there are places to put them."The findings suggest that expanding chip production alone may not be enough to sustain the AI boom unless companies can also secure electricity, suitable land and operational data centres.Morgan Stanley said access to electricity was increasingly favouring large companies with strong financial backing and predictable revenues."We believe we're in an environment where data center energization is being concentrated across a handful of large, credit-worthy players," the report stated.It added that companies with strong credit support and large power requirements were securing electricity more quickly, potentially leaving smaller developers at a disadvantage.The research estimated that major technology companies and specialist cloud providers could account for approximately 94 per cent of global data-centre capacity additions in 2026, followed by 64 per cent in 2027 and 57 per cent in 2028."We believe this could potentially 'squeeze out' or put pressure on other players over time," Morgan Stanley said.The constraints could also affect semiconductor manufacturers if data centres are unable to install the chips they have ordered."If there's chip capacity expected to come online that cannot be deployed at data centers, we could see customers push out delivery or start canceling orders," the report warned.However, Morgan Stanley expects Nvidia and Broadcom to meet their 2027 forecasts, citing their visibility into customer demand and infrastructure availability. It sees greater risks for suppliers of memory chips, optical equipment and other supporting components if deployment slows.The report also indicated that the infrastructure challenge could persist beyond 2028, with the projected cumulative US data-centre power shortfall potentially widening to 68 GW by 2029.The shortage could encourage technology companies to expand computing infrastructure outside the United States, including in Asian markets such as India.Morgan Stanley's Asia data-centre team estimates that 14 GW of demand from US hyperscalers could shift to Asia through 2030, although the report does not specify India's share."While we expect international expansion to continue, we don't see it as a solution to the US power problem," the report said.The findings underline a growing challenge for the AI industry: technological advances and spending on chips may not translate into additional computing capacity unless electricity supply and supporting infrastructure expand at a similar pace.

Indian Firm Develops Wideband HF Modem Under iDEX
articles.text:
Indian technology company Cyronics Innovation Labs Ltd has revealed its collaboration with Indian Air Force for the indigenous development of Wideband High Frequency (HF) Modem under the umbrella of Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) under the Ministry of Defence.
The development aligns with the company’s aims to provide cutting-edge communications technology for mission-critical defence applications, it said. It has not revealed the number of modems that have been supplied or the value of the contract or the platforms and units in the Indian Air Force that will be using the modem.
The importance of HF communications is still present in military applications, as it can provide long-distance communication beyond the line of sight, even if satellite connectivity or conventional communications infrastructure are not available or functioning. In some circumstances, forces spread across different locations can communicate via HF links, an alternative communication route to the traditional VHF path.
A wideband HF modem is one which can support digital data at a wider radio-frequency bandwidth than standard narrowband modems. This can aid higher data rates, but throughput and reliability vary depending on the bandwidth and the propagation conditions, the quality of interference, the antenna systems and the radio equipment the modem is integrated with.
Resilient Communications are crucial in the Indian Air Force for ensuring seamless connectivity among geographically dispersed bases and units deployed in the field. Indian developers might also have more flexibility in adapting the equipment to service needs through indigenous modem technology and also carry out the modification of equipment and become less reliant on overseas suppliers. The amount of these benefits will vary based on the system’s proven efficacy and ability to integrate into the current communications infrastructure.
Cyronics stated that it has designed the Wideband HF Modem under the iDEX framework, which is a government initiative to motivate start-ups and industry to innovate and create defence technologies. The programme offers a pathway for the domestic industry to collaborate on capability gaps in the military and to create solutions that can be evaluated by the military.
No technical data such as frequency range, maximum data rate, waveform, encryption and anti-jamming performance, environmental qualification is included in the announcement. It also does not indicate if the system is in use as part of a user trial or if it has been formally certified or if it is in operational service.
Those bits of information would have been key to evaluating the modem’s performance and what future it might hold in the Air Force’s communications system. Good for wideband alone isn’t good for secure or interference resistant radio, it takes the whole radio system to make that happen, including the waveforms, signal processing and security.

articles.text:
Boeing [NYSE: BA] announced the winners of the 11th annual Boeing National Aeromodeling Competition, one of India’s largest and most popular aeromodeling programs designed for aspiring aerospace engineers. This year, the competition drew more than 1,179 students representing 115 institutions across India.
46 finalists from 14 teams were selected for the finale held at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi. Three teams were declared winners of the competition.
Salil Gupte, President, Boeing India & South Asia, said, “Now in its eleventh year, this competition has continued to grow into India’s largest aeromodeling platform, giving students an opportunity to turn their passion for aviation and engineering into hands-on experience. Participants design, build, test, and fly fixed-wing aircraft models under defined performance, safety, and mission criteria.
This year, the students were given a challenge to focus on a “collaborative humanitarian airlift mission” that evaluated aircraft design, flight stability, payload integration, and coordinated mission execution across paired teams.
Over the years, Boeing has strategically invested in helping nurture talent for the aerospace sector in India. Its programs, including Boeing University Innovation Leadership Development (BUILD), past programs such as the Boeing HorizonX India Innovation Challenge and the Accelerated Aircraft Maintenance Engineers (AME) Apprenticeship program have continued to empower entrepreneurs and are helping build a skilled workforce for the country’s aerospace and defence sector.

Amazon wants you to Bee-lieve wearable AI can recall it all for you
articles.text: Amazon wants to ensure you have a personal AI that you can carry with you anywhere, listening in on your conversations so it can remind you of key details – and give you personalized shopping recommendations, of course. The global online bazaar has unveiled two new AI-based products from Bee, a startup in wearable devices that it acquired last year in a deal said to be worth $300 million. Bee’s original product for Amazon was tried out and sort of given approval by friend of The Register Corey Quinn, Chief Cloud Economist at Duckbill, earlier this year. One new gizmo, Bee Frontier, is designed to be worn like a watch or one of those fitness trackers, although to our mind it looks more like you are wearing a doorbell. The other, Bee Eclipse, is a slimline and lightweight device about the size of a credit card that attaches to the back of your phone magnetically, like a limpet. Both are intended to listen in to your conversations and help you remember important details, like when you are meeting your friend for a pint later and at which hospitality outlet. The devices take note of the details you might otherwise forget, and then turn them into useful conversation summaries, to-dos and reminders, Amazon says. The pair of devices feature a single button to turn on or off, and a visible indicator that lights up when one is listening in and its AI is summarizing the conversation. When enabled, the eavesdropper gathers context from your conversations to provide insights and recommendations. Summaries of your conversations can be accessed via a Bee mobile app on iPhone or Android (linked via Bluetooth), or an all-new desktop app. These can be organized using templates for things such as lectures, or users can just review memories from the past few days to see what you discussed. The Bee devices pick up on trends or themes that recur, and recommend personalized goals and actions. That sounds alarm bells for us, as it suggests the AI is designed to get to know you, and what you like. Along with the new hardware, Bee has now gained the ability to connect to Amazon’s Alexa+ AI assistant and Amazon.com, which means that you can ask Alexa for a meeting summary - or get personalized shopping recommendations from Amazon based on what your personal earwig has gleaned. However, Amazon says that the latest Bee products respect user privacy, as audio is processed into insights in real time and not stored, while transcripts are encrypted and only the user can access them. Bee Frontier is claimed to have IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, and has a USB-C charging port. Bee Eclipse also has a USB-C port but is said to last for more than 21 days of use from a single battery charge. Both devices come in a choice of colors, with Bee Frontier available now for $74.99 and Bee Eclipse due to be available shortly for $99.99. ®

Get in the bin! UK Space Agency wants public to name its debris removal mission
articles.text: The UK Space Agency needs a name for its Active Debris Removal Mission and has decided that the great British public are the people for the job. The agency confirmed the operation earlier this week and selected ClearSpace UK to lead it. The plan is to remove two UK-registered satellites from Low Earth Orbit, with the clean-up due to begin in 2029. The UK government is backing the effort with more than £60 million, and it expects the disposal to be completed by 2032. The spacecraft will grab each satellite, drop it into a lower orbit for disposal by burning up in the Earth's atmosphe, then climb to a higher one to await its next job. Less suicide dive, more cosmic bin round. And because it’s refuellable, the UK government says it "can help make a difference and sweep space for years to come." Launch is planned from SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland. But first, the quest needs a name. The Active Debris Removal Mission hardly trips off the tongue, and the UK Space Agency gave inspirational examples of other project names, such as NASA's Mercury program (named after the Roman god) or Tim Peake's Principia mission (inspired by Sir Isaac Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica). Oddly, the agency didn't mention the poll to brand a scientific research ship, which was eventually named Sir David Attenborough rather than Boaty McBoatface, the most popular suggestion. The tag must consist of two words – so no "Itsy bitsy teeny weeny orbit debris clear machiney" – and 150 words to explain the name and how it reflects the theme. So no backronyms, for example Broom (British Robotic Orbital Object Manipulator). Starry McBinface? Obviously, swear words are not allowed, nor is anything deemed "potentially offensive" or political. Using anything that might attract copyright or intellectual property lawyers is also out. Letting the public suggest a name feels potentially riskier than the mission itself, though it should generate some engagement. It's a high-risk, high-reward campaign; there are plenty of dead satellites cluttering orbit, and the ability to remove them is becoming increasingly important. Rob Atchison, Managing Director of ClearSpace UK, said, "Our next step is to design, build and test a spacecraft that can get close, safely, to an object never designed to be caught, and take control of it." If you're getting a sense of déjà vu about this expedition, you're probably right. The European Space Agency (ESA) announced ClearSpace-1 in 2019, which the agency called "the first space mission to remove an item of debris from orbit" with a launch set for 2025. At the time, ClearSpace founder and CEO Luc Piguet said: "This is the right time for such a mission." In latest announcement, Piguet called the UKSA's selection "an important milestone." This is far from the first mission to grapple an object in orbit. Most recently, Katalyst Space sent its LINK spacecraft to rescue NASA's Swift observatory. That was intended to capture the Swift spacecraft and raise its altitude, but failures with LINK doomed it. Perhaps things might have gone better if the public had been given an opportunity to name the spacecraft? ®

Self-improving data synthesis enables scalable adaptation of embedding models
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.14730v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AI agents require specialised retrieval across domains and tasks, but adapting embedding models is constrained by costly manual training-data design. Here we introduce SYNTRA, a self-improving agentic framework that turns a few retrieval examples into reusable synthesis instructions. Given an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs, SYNTRA infers implicit information needs and relevance criteria, then uses feedback on trial outputs to refine instructions for query generation and relevance assessment. Experiments across 24 datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate that the same synthesis workflow produces effective training data, benefiting even strong embedding models with and without existing labelled training sets. Self-improvement strengthens this supervision on all six evaluated tasks, yielding better retrieval than human calibration on four. The training value persists at larger scales: on MS MARCO, retrieval gains continue across a 32-fold range of synthetic training-data sizes. SYNTRA thus enables scalable embedding-model adaptation with minimal human intervention.
